edition.deck: A failed execution leaves Christa Pike in pain; a fragile Ukraine ceasefire enables an evacuation; and Russia’s last major independent newspaper prepares to close.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritise significant developments from the day, including fresh reporting on the Ukraine ceasefire, Russia’s shrinking space for independent journalism, and new Danish and UK policy developments. Treat claims and forecasts with care, especially where investigations or decisions remain unresolved.

content.headline: Christa Pike says she remains in pain after failed Tennessee execution
content.shortHeadline: Christa Pike describes pain after failed execution
content.standfirst: Pike says she has struggled with constant pain since surviving two injections during a botched execution in September. Tennessee has paused executions while an independent review examines what happened.

image.caption: Christa Pike enters a criminal court in Knoxville, Tennessee.

sources.originalTitle: Christa Pike makes first public comments since failed execution: ‘There is pain in my mind and in my soul’
US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
Dødsdømt efter mislykket henrettelse: 'Min krop gør ondt'

segments.body: Christa Pike says she has not been free of pain since she survived an execution attempt in Tennessee on 30 September. “My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak,” she said in her first public statement since the failed lethal injection.

segments.title: What happens next
segments.body: Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995, when Pike was 18. She has returned to prison after hospital treatment. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has paused executions for the rest of the year and ordered an independent review; he has said he expects Pike’s sentence to remain unless the courts decide otherwise.

content.headline: Ceasefire enables evacuation from devastated Russian-occupied Oleshky
content.shortHeadline: Evacuation leaves hundreds in Russian-occupied Oleshky
content.standfirst: Hundreds left the frontline town during a four-hour window, but several hundred more are understood to have stayed without gas, electricity or running water. The fragile truce is due to end on Sunday.

image.caption: A report on the evacuation from Russian-occupied Oleshky.

sources.originalTitle: Ceasefire allows evacuation from devastated Russian-occupied Oleshky

segments.body: Hundreds of residents were evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky after a humanitarian ceasefire opened a route out of the devastated town. A convoy of 25 buses was available to take up to 750 people, while ambulances helped those with limited mobility. The evacuation was confirmed by Russian and Ukrainian authorities.

segments.title: Those who stayed
segments.body: Several hundred residents are understood to have remained, despite shortages of basic services. Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman said those who stayed would be offered humanitarian assistance. One resident told the BBC she would not leave because she could not take her animals.

segments.title: A limited pause
segments.body: The ceasefire, in force across the Kherson frontline region since Tuesday, is due to end on Sunday. The BBC reports concerns among some residents that the pause could give Russian forces time to build up their presence near the Dnipro river. Moscow has said the local truce should not be taken as a sign it is ready to extend a ceasefire across Ukraine.

content.headline: Russia’s Novaya Gazeta says mounting pressure has forced it to close
content.shortHeadline: Novaya Gazeta to close under pressure from Russian authorities
content.standfirst: The independent newspaper says an eviction order, the loss of reader donations and legal restrictions have made it impossible to continue. It was one of the last critical outlets still operating inside Russia.

image.caption: The Novaya Gazeta office building on the day the newspaper announced its closure.

sources.originalTitle: Russian society being ‘systematically crushed’ says Novaya Gazeta as newspaper announces closure
Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities

segments.body: Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent newspapers, says it will close next month after mounting pressure from the authorities. The paper says it has lost its newsroom, its donation platforms and its legal right to publish. Its editor, Sergei Sokolov, described the closure as part of a wider effort to crush Russian society.

segments.title: A shrinking space for reporting
segments.body: The newspaper built its reputation on investigations into corruption and human rights abuses. Six journalists connected with it have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, censorship laws and the loss of its publishing licence forced the paper to stop printing; staff continued with a reduced operation and a limited print run.

The latest pressure includes an order to leave its Moscow offices by 9 November, the closure of donation services and the arrest of investigative journalist Oleg Roldugin. Staff say they may try to find a way to continue their work, but have not set out how they could fund it.

content.headline: US tech shares slide as investors question the cost of the AI boom
content.shortHeadline: Tech stocks fall as investors question AI spending
content.standfirst: Intel, Amazon, Reddit and Roblox shares fell as companies’ investment plans and results unsettled investors. The Nasdaq opened at its lowest level in more than two months, extending a sharp sell-off across major technology stocks.

image.caption: A view of the New York Stock Exchange.

sources.originalTitle: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears

segments.body: US technology shares fell as investors weighed the cost of building out artificial intelligence against the returns so far. The Nasdaq opened down 2.5% on Friday, its lowest level in more than two months. Intel shares fell as much as 30% after it warned of a weaker computer market while planning to increase AI spending.

segments.title: Pressure across the sector
segments.body: Amazon shares fell after its reported earnings missed expectations and it disclosed higher spending. Reddit also dropped after reporting weaker daily user figures and warning that AI-driven search was reducing referral traffic; Roblox shares fell as daily active users declined. Alphabet continued to slide after a sharp fall the previous day.

Analysts are questioning whether the huge investments in AI will produce enough returns. Intel’s finance chief said the company did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast a continuing slowdown in the PC market through at least the first half of next year.

content.headline: US judges accuse Trump administration of election interference and overreach
content.shortHeadline: Judges rebuke Trump administration over election and court cases
content.standfirst: Several federal judges have sharply criticised government actions, including a bid to set aside ballots in California. The administration rejects the accusations, and the disputes are continuing through the courts.

image.caption: A report on the Trump administration’s legal actions involving voter rolls.

sources.originalTitle: Furious US judges are lashing out at Trump as he ‘puts democracy in danger’

segments.body: A California federal judge rejected the Trump administration’s request to segregate about 20,000 ballots it said may have been sent to non-citizens. Judge David Carter said the government’s case threatened voting rights and described it as part of a wider pattern of attempted election interference. The Justice Department said it was following the facts and the law.

segments.title: Other disputes
segments.body: The report also details judges’ criticism of the Justice Department in separate cases, including a complaint about the handling of a case involving two former FBI officials. A judge in Washington accused the government of pressing ahead with work on a public golf course while the matter was before the courts.

The account draws on rulings and reporting about a series of legal disputes, but their outcomes remain unresolved. In the California case, the judge ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening officials who did not comply with its requests.

content.headline: US military briefing fuels speculation of renewed strikes on Iran
content.shortHeadline: US considers next steps in Iran war after general’s briefing
content.standfirst: The head of US Central Command briefed Donald Trump on the conflict and possible next steps, according to reporting cited by The i Paper. Fresh strikes have not been announced, and diplomatic efforts are continuing.

image.caption: US Central Command oversees American forces in the Middle East.

sources.originalTitle: The two major clues Trump could soon resume Iran strikes

segments.body: US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper briefed President Donald Trump and senior officials on the Iran conflict and possible next steps, according to The i Paper’s account of reporting by the Wall Street Journal. The briefing has added to speculation that Washington may consider renewed military action, but no new strikes have been announced.

segments.title: Risks and diplomacy
segments.body: Reports cited in the article say the US has warned regional allies to prepare for possible strikes after the midterm elections, while moving some forces and assets around the region. An attack could prompt Iranian retaliation. Regional governments have called for diplomacy, and Iran says it is still giving negotiations a chance; the sides remain divided over sanctions and the Strait of Hormuz.

content.headline: Six people killed in helicopter crash in India’s Uttarakhand state
content.shortHeadline: Six die in helicopter crash near India pilgrimage site
content.standfirst: Five pilgrims and the pilot died after a helicopter went down near Badrinath, officials say. The cause is unknown; reports cite heavy rain and poor visibility, while the safety of pilgrimage flights is under scrutiny.

image.caption: Joshimath, near the area where the helicopter was reported missing.

sources.originalTitle: Six dead after helicopter crashes in northern Indian state

segments.body: Five pilgrims and a pilot have died after a helicopter crashed in Uttarakhand, northern India, officials say. It had reportedly taken off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday before losing contact. The cause has not been established; the region had reports of heavy rain and poor visibility.

segments.title: Safety concerns
segments.body: Helicopter services are increasingly used by pilgrims travelling to mountain shrines, but a series of accidents has prompted scrutiny. Before Friday’s crash, India’s weather department had issued an orange alert warning of thunderstorms, hail and strong winds in the area.

content.headline: Alaska Senate candidate denies role in alleged ballot scheme
content.shortHeadline: Peltola denies involvement in alleged Alaska ballot plot
content.standfirst: Mary Peltola says she knew nothing of an alleged effort to recruit a second Dan Sullivan to the Senate race. The Justice Department has issued subpoenas, but no charges have been filed and the allegations have not been independently verified by the BBC.

image.caption: Mary Peltola speaks to voters during the Alaska Senate campaign.

sources.originalTitle: Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot

segments.body: Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied knowing about an alleged effort to recruit another candidate named Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s close Senate race. The incumbent, Republican Dan S. Sullivan, and his allies say the move was intended to confuse voters. Peltola said she had no interest in tricking them.

segments.title: Investigation and legal challenge
segments.body: The New York Times reported that people connected to Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee tried to recruit Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher. The BBC says it has not independently verified that reporting. The Justice Department has issued subpoenas, but no charges have been filed. A separate federal lawsuit seeks to prevent certification of the result if the incumbent loses.

content.headline: Poundland seeks a rescue as administration and store closures loom
content.shortHeadline: Poundland faces administration as rescue talks continue
content.standfirst: The chain has sought protection from creditors while a solution is explored. With suppliers holding back deliveries and buyers circling parts of the business, up to 12,000 staff face uncertainty ahead of Christmas.

image.caption: Poundland’s options are being assessed as the retailer seeks a way forward.

sources.originalTitle: Poundland in peril: how rampant inflation and price wars left £1 stores exposed

segments.body: Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, giving the retailer 10 days’ protection from creditors as it seeks a solution. The chain operates about 600 stores, including Dealz in Ireland, and employs up to 12,000 people. Suppliers are holding back deliveries, adding to pressure on the business.

segments.title: A difficult sale
segments.body: Its US owner, Gordon Brothers, rejected a management-backed offer from Martin Property Group, understood to be worth about £15m, and is also considering offers for parts of the chain. Some established retailers have offered to take on groups of stores, but a sale of the whole business has not been secured.

segments.title: Why the model is under strain
segments.body: The retailer’s former single-price proposition has been squeezed by inflation in goods, labour and energy, while budget rivals and online sellers intensify competition. Poundland’s pre-tax loss widened to £85.3m in the year to September 2025. The company has also acknowledged mistakes, including introducing clothing ranges that proved unpopular with UK shoppers.

content.headline: Driver found guilty of murdering cyclist dragged beneath his car
content.shortHeadline: Driver convicted of murder after dragging cyclist for a mile
content.standfirst: Simon Richardson was convicted after driving on with headteacher Michael Mullins trapped under his car, the court heard. Richardson denied knowing Mullins was there; sentencing is due on Monday.

image.caption: Simon Richardson’s car after the fatal collision.

sources.originalTitle: Man who ran over cyclist and dragged him under car for a mile convicted of murder

segments.body: Simon Richardson, 35, has been found guilty of murdering cyclist Michael Mullins, 56, after a collision in Greater Manchester in April. Prosecutors said Richardson drove for more than a mile with Mullins trapped under his car, knowing he was there. Richardson denied realising the cyclist was beneath the vehicle.

segments.title: Evidence at trial
segments.body: The court heard that Richardson drove to a secluded track, where he tried to dislodge Mullins before driving away. A motorcyclist later found Mullins on a grass verge, but emergency services could not save him. Richardson’s passenger told the trial they heard moaning and that he said, “He’s under the car.”
Mullins’ family said he was devoted to them and that his death had left a gap in their lives and at Stretford Grammar School, where he was headteacher. Richardson will be sentenced on Monday.

content.headline: Police watchdog opens investigation into Met’s handling of 2019 letter
content.shortHeadline: Watchdog investigates Met over letter alleging overseas offences
content.standfirst: The IOPC will examine why the Metropolitan Police did not pass on allegations in a 2019 letter to relevant overseas authorities. The claims are under investigation and are not findings of wrongdoing by Thomas Markle.

image.caption: A report on the 2019 letter to the Metropolitan Police.

sources.originalTitle: Police watchdog to investigate Met’s handling of Meghan warning letter

segments.body: The Independent Office for Police Conduct has opened an investigation into how the Metropolitan Police handled a 2019 letter containing allegations of serious offending overseas by Thomas Markle, the father of the Duchess of Sussex. The IOPC says the Met failed to pass the claims to relevant authorities at the time.

segments.title: What the watchdog will examine
segments.body: The investigation will consider who in the Met made decisions about the letter and whether police policies were followed. The watchdog has decided not to investigate a separate question about whether passing the letter to the Duchess of Sussex’s office breached data rules. The Met is now sending details to authorities in the US, the Philippines and Thailand.

Markle denies child sexual abuse allegations and is under investigation by authorities in the Philippines. The claims in the letter are distinct from any findings by police; the IOPC’s inquiry concerns the Met’s handling of the information it received in 2019.

content.headline: UK bars Swedish climate academic Andreas Malm from entering the country
content.shortHeadline: UK travel ban on Andreas Malm sparks free-speech row
content.standfirst: Malm says he has not been told why his travel authorisation was cancelled and suspects his planned appearance with Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori is the reason. The Home Office says it cannot discuss individual cases.

image.caption: Swedish climate academic Andreas Malm.

sources.originalTitle: Andreas Malm condemns UK travel ban as ‘drift into authoritarianism’
Climate academic Andreas Malm barred from entering UK

segments.body: Swedish academic Andreas Malm says the UK has revoked his electronic travel authorisation, telling him his presence was “not considered to be conducive to the public good”. He was due to speak at a London event next week alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the proscribed group Palestine Action.

segments.title: Competing explanations
segments.body: Malm said he had no concrete evidence for the reason and denied supporting or financing Palestine Action. He said he would appear by video link. The Home Office would not discuss an individual case, but a source said cancellations on public-good grounds are based on an assessment of potential risk to UK society.

segments.title: Criticism and uncertainty
segments.body: The decision has drawn criticism from writers and politicians, who describe it as an attack on free expression. Malm also raised the possibility that his past comments about the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks could be relevant, but said those views had long been public. The government has not confirmed its reasons.

content.headline: UK trial tests five-day radiotherapy course for early breast cancer
content.shortHeadline: Trial tests five-day breast cancer radiotherapy course
content.standfirst: More than 1,000 people have joined a UK trial testing whether treatment can be shortened from three weeks to five days. Researchers hope it could reduce hospital visits, but results are not expected until 2033.

image.caption: A government-funded trial is testing a shorter course of breast cancer radiotherapy.

sources.originalTitle: The radical new breast cancer trials to cut gruelling radiotherapy sessions by two-thirds

segments.body: A UK trial is testing whether radiotherapy for early-stage breast cancer can be delivered safely over five days rather than three weeks. More than 1,000 people have joined so far, and the study aims to recruit more than 4,000 participants across 39 hospitals.

segments.title: What the trial will measure
segments.body: The FAST-Forward Boost trial adds a targeted dose of radiation to the shorter course, aiming to help prevent cancer returning. Participants will be followed for five years, with results expected in 2033. If the approach proves safe and effective, fewer hospital visits could ease the burden on patients and free NHS capacity.

content.headline: Budget’s £100 energy payment reaches some higher-income areas too
content.shortHeadline: £100 energy payment criticised for blunt eligibility rules
content.standfirst: The one-off payment will go to households in council tax bands A to D, regardless of income. Critics say that can include affluent households while excluding some people in need who live in higher-banded homes.

image.caption: A Wandsworth resident says the £100 payment may be quickly absorbed by winter costs.

sources.originalTitle: The 10 wealthiest areas where thousands will get £100 energy payout
The affluent London suburb where people will receive £100 in their bank accounts for free

segments.body: The government’s £100 Household Energy Payment will go to households in council tax bands A to D, with the money due to be paid from January 2027. The scheme is intended to help with rising energy bills and will reach about 20 million households in England, according to the reports.

segments.title: Who qualifies
segments.body: Eligibility is based on council tax bands, not household income. Reporting from Wandsworth, where many residents earn above the London average, illustrates how some higher-income households may qualify. Campaigners say people in need who live in homes in higher bands could miss out.

The government says the scheme will reach many fuel-stressed and low-income households. Critics argue it is poorly targeted and may not cover the expected increase in bills. The £100 payment is one part of a wider Budget package that also includes scrapping gas standing charges.

content.headline: Ministers weigh changes to benefits for young people as reform plans take shape
content.shortHeadline: Youth benefit changes under consideration as reforms take shape
content.standfirst: Possible changes include tighter access to health-related Universal Credit for under-25s and more employment support. Ministers have not settled the package, and longer-term support may take years to reduce spending.

image.caption: The government is considering changes to benefits and employment support for young people.

sources.originalTitle: The benefit cuts that are now more likely
Benefits overhaul for Neets will take 10 years to complete under ‘Labour way’

segments.body: The government is considering changes to benefits for young people as it prepares responses to reviews on youth unemployment and disability benefits. The options described include restricting the health element of Universal Credit for under-25s and expanding employment support, but no final package has been announced.

segments.title: Different routes, different timelines
segments.body: Economists cited by The i Paper say reducing eligibility could produce savings sooner, while employment programmes would require upfront spending and may take five to 10 years to affect the public finances. The review led by Alan Milburn is expected to set out a longer-term plan; a separate review is considering disability benefits.

The reporting notes that proposals could affect young people with health conditions or disabilities, including those receiving additional Universal Credit support. Ministers say reform should help people into work rather than rely on what the Prime Minister calls crude cuts. The exact eligibility rules and timetable remain undecided.

content.headline: EU pause puts Denmark’s planned social-media age limit in doubt
content.shortHeadline: EU pause puts Denmark’s planned age limit on social media at risk
content.standfirst: The European Commission says it will pause approval of national rules that overlap with planned EU-wide regulations. A Danish lawmaker expects Denmark’s 2027 plan to be affected, but the government has not confirmed its position.

image.caption: The European Commission is working on a common European approach to social-media age limits.

sources.originalTitle: Ny EU-udmelding truer regeringens plan for aldersgrænse på sociale medier

segments.body: Denmark’s planned age limit of 15 for social media use from July 2027 is in doubt after the European Commission said it would pause approval of national rules that overlap with future EU-wide regulations for 12 months. The Commission says it wants to work towards common European rules.

segments.title: What remains unclear
segments.body: Danish MEP Christel Schaldemose expects Denmark to be covered by the pause because its legislation has not been finally adopted. She says a common EU law could take years to come into effect. The Danish ministry responsible has not yet confirmed whether the national plan is affected or whether Denmark could receive an exception.

Children’s rights organisation Børns Vilkår says children will lose out if the national measure is delayed, while agreeing that a common EU approach would be preferable. The Commission’s proposal would bar children under 13 from social media and limit access for those aged 13 to 15.

content.headline: Man given life sentence for 2020 double murder linked to Danish gang
content.shortHeadline: Man sentenced to life for gang-linked double murder in Kalundborg
content.standfirst: A court found the 29-year-old took part in planning a revenge attack that killed two men and seriously injured a third. He has appealed, and his identity remains protected by a court order.

image.caption: Archive image accompanying coverage of the gang-linked case.

sources.originalTitle: LTF'er er blevet idømt livstid for dobbeltdrab i bandemiljøet

segments.body: A 29-year-old man has been sentenced to life in prison for a double murder and attempted murder linked to the gang Loyal To Familia. The shootings took place in a Kalundborg supermarket car park in November 2020. The court found that he had actively helped plan the attack.

segments.title: The case
segments.body: The court heard that the attack was planned in a group chat as revenge for the abduction of a gang member. Two men died and a third was critically injured. The defendant denied guilt and said he had left the gang; the court rejected his account as untrustworthy and constructed.

The man has appealed, seeking acquittal or a reduced sentence. His identity is covered by a court order. Six other men have previously received life sentences in connection with the killings and attempted murder; proceedings involving other defendants remain ongoing.

content.headline: Danish Industry chief’s cloned voice used in attempted €3.3m fraud
content.shortHeadline: AI-cloned voice used in attempted €3.3m Danish Industry fraud
content.standfirst: A staff member in South Korea was asked to transfer about $500,000 after a caller impersonated director Lars Sandahl Sørensen. Internal checks stopped the payment; experts say voice and video cloning can make such scams more convincing.

image.caption: Lars Sandahl Sørensen says the incident shows the need to prepare for new kinds of cyber threat.

sources.originalTitle: Svindelforsøg var så overbevisende, at det kunne have snydt DI-direktørs mor
Svindlere kan nemt klone og misbruge din chefs stemme eller ansigt: 'Det er ikke science fiction længere'

segments.body: A staff member at Danish Industry’s office in South Korea was targeted by a caller using an AI-generated imitation of director Lars Sandahl Sørensen’s voice. The caller asked for about $500,000, equivalent to 3.3 million Danish kroner, to be transferred in connection with a purported confidential business deal. Internal checks stopped the payment.

segments.title: How the approach worked
segments.body: After claiming the phone connection was poor, the impersonator moved the conversation to WhatsApp, using a profile with Sørensen’s name and picture. Danish Industry says the caller appeared to know details of the supposed transaction. The organisation has reported the incident to police.

segments.title: Checks and precautions
segments.body: Technology analysts interviewed by DR say AI can now imitate a person’s voice and, in some cases, appearance in real time. They advise treating payment requests with suspicion, requiring a second colleague to approve transfers, and agreeing a family password for personal calls. Police advise against sharing personal information or transferring money over the phone.

content.headline: Danish sales of wood-burning stoves rise as households seek backup heat
content.shortHeadline: More Danes buy wood stoves for backup heat and lower bills
content.standfirst: Industry figures show sales rose in the first half of 2026, with buyers citing energy prices and concern about power cuts. Older stoves are also being replaced or removed under rules aimed at reducing harmful emissions.

image.caption: Niels Ole Frederiksen installed a wood-burning stove as a backup in case of a power cut.

sources.originalTitle: Flere beholder brændeovnen som en backup-løsning

segments.body: Sales of wood-burning stoves and fireplace inserts rose in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, according to the Danish industry association DAPO. It reports sales up 7% for stoves and 12% for inserts among its members.

segments.title: A backup source of heat
segments.body: Buyers and retailers told DR they are looking for a way to heat their homes if electricity fails, as well as a way to manage energy costs. One homeowner in western Zealand said he had installed a stove as a backup alongside an air-to-water heat pump.

Industry representatives also say the replacement rules for older stoves contribute to sales: new owners of homes with stoves made before 2003 must replace or remove them. The association expects demand to continue rising, though the report does not separate how much of the increase is due to preparedness, energy prices or replacement requirements.

content.headline: Danish debate over European leaders’ calls with Putin exposes split on dialogue
content.shortHeadline: Danish debate over calls to Putin reveals split on diplomacy
content.standfirst: A defence editor says European leaders should speak with Russia’s president, while former foreign minister Jeppe Kofod argues dialogue needs a shared purpose and coordination. The dispute follows criticism from Mette Frederiksen.

image.caption: Olfi editor Peter Ernstved Rasmussen argues for European leaders talking with Putin.

sources.originalTitle: 'Man behøver ikke at sige ’hold kæft’, men ...'

segments.body: A Danish debate has opened over whether European leaders should talk directly with Vladimir Putin. Mette Frederiksen criticised the Finnish and Norwegian leaders after they spoke with the Russian president, saying Europe should stay united rather than act alone. Defence outlet Olfi’s editor Peter Ernstved Rasmussen argues that some European leaders are right to talk to Putin.

segments.title: A question of purpose
segments.body: Former foreign minister Jeppe Kofod says dialogue must have a clear diplomatic purpose and be coordinated among EU countries. He argues that past attempts failed because Putin set terms that required accepting Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and says any talks should be backed by military and economic strength.

Rasmussen says countries bordering Russia have reason to speak with its president and warns against ignoring Russia’s nuclear arsenal. He argues that continuing the war risks further escalation and suffering. The disagreement is over whether engagement can help, and what conditions would make it meaningful.

content.headline: Skepta says his new album puts conscious messages over a grime pulse
content.shortHeadline: Skepta brings a more conscious voice to his new album
content.standfirst: The grime star says fatherhood and a reckoning with past mistakes shaped The Fork and Knife, his first solo album since 2019. He also discusses immigration, multicultural Britain and the responsibility that comes with his voice.

image.caption: Skepta, whose new album draws on his reflections about music and responsibility.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Ignorance towards immigration is horrible. It’s not British’: Skepta on his long-awaited return – and his anger at the racist right

segments.body: Skepta says The Fork and Knife, due next week, took seven years to make because he wanted to be more mindful about what he says. The 15-track album still makes room for grime and party music, but he describes its aim as delivering conscious messages “but still have a vibe”.

segments.title: A British story
segments.body: On “Innocent Smile”, featuring Madness singer Suggs, Skepta draws on his family’s Nigerian heritage and the multicultural life he grew up with in Tottenham. He says his father played ska at home and remembers Black people and skinheads meeting at east London parties. The interview also revisits his apologies for past missteps, including the 2024 album artwork that inadvertently evoked the Holocaust.

content.headline: Bombstrap lead a week of new tracks with Rotterdam’s uncompromising punk
content.shortHeadline: Bombstrap lead this week’s new tracks with Rotterdam punk
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s weekly selection introduces the theatrical noise of Bombstrap, led by vocalist and visual artist Eva Kah, alongside seven new tracks spanning house, jazz, techno-pop and dream pop.

image.caption: Eva Kah of Bombstrap, the Rotterdam band featured in this week’s new-track selection.

sources.originalTitle: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: Dutch squat-punks Bombstrap’s uncompromising racket

segments.body: Rotterdam band Bombstrap draw on hardcore punk, art-school eccentricity and the communal squatting scene around Het Poortgebouw. The Guardian’s feature describes their debut Big Enemy as a shifting, high-volume sound, led by Eva Kah’s confrontational performance and an attitude at odds with the city’s gentrification.

segments.title: More new sounds
segments.body: The playlist moves well beyond punk: Clementine Douglas brings deep vocal house, DJ Heartstring pair breakbeats with spoken-word passages, and saxophonist Josh Johnson sets two melodic motifs against analogue synth. Other picks include bright techno-pop from Isaac Kniveton, shoegaze-leaning Anamanaguchi, Japanese artist Metoronori and a new lullaby from Waterbaby.

content.headline: Radie Peat’s solo debut turns traditional songs into startling testimony
content.shortHeadline: Radie Peat gives traditional songs startling force
content.standfirst: The Lankum singer’s first solo album gathers songs of women’s suffering and endurance, from a battered wife’s divided loyalties to a lament for Ireland. The review praises its spare arrangements and visceral performances.

image.caption: Radie Peat, whose solo debut reworks traditional songs of struggle and endurance.

sources.originalTitle: Radie Peat: No Human Tongue Can Tell review – Lankum singer’s solo debut is the year’s best folk album

segments.body: On No Human Tongue Can Tell, Radie Peat begins with a stark voice and subtle piano before adding layers of Mellotron and Wurlitzer. The review finds a unifying theme of female struggle, strength and endurance in a collection that draws much of its power from songs Peat has performed for years.

segments.title: Songs that carry their history
segments.body: Peat gives “Willow Garden” the weight of a haunting elegy, while “Still I Love Him” holds the tension of a woman emotionally bound to the husband who beats her. “Dark Horse on the Wind”, Liam Weldon’s lament for the lost dream of the Irish republic, ends the review’s examples on a stark note. Producer John “Spud” Murphy’s textures bring out the detail of Peat’s concertina and Eleanor Myler’s drums.

content.headline: Kali Malone finds a more direct, emotionally charged sound on Burning Song
content.shortHeadline: Kali Malone turns toward emotion on Burning Song
content.standfirst: The US drone composer takes a more compact approach on her new album, recorded on the Bach organ at Leipzig’s Thomaskirche. The review hears a sombre, carefully controlled shift toward direct feeling.

image.caption: Kali Malone, whose new album uses the Bach organ at Leipzig’s Thomaskirche.

sources.originalTitle: Kali Malone: Burning Song review – drone composer wields Bach’s organ to breathtaking effect

segments.body: Burning Song is unusually compact by Kali Malone’s standards: its pieces are shorter than the extended works that established her reputation, and it sets aside the contrapuntal canon form. Malone plays the Bach organ at Leipzig’s Thomaskirche with cellist Lucy Railton and bowed-guitar player Stephen O’Malley.

segments.title: Attention in the details
segments.body: The review describes the trio’s sound as a close interplay of crackle, breath and scrape. “Grieving Figure” moves from a distant, sustained note toward a brighter finish, while “Bells on a Branch” ends in a dry, depleted mood. The album’s emotional directness, the critic argues, remains restrained rather than reaching for easy grandeur.

content.headline: CDs find new listeners as fans look for music beyond streaming
content.shortHeadline: Why CDs are finding listeners again
content.standfirst: Searches for CD players at John Lewis are up 96% since July, while a separate report found CD sales up 16%. Music fans explain what physical discs offer that streaming does not: ownership, focus and a more deliberate way to listen.

image.caption: Young people choosing CDs in a music shop in Munich.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comeback

segments.body: The Guardian reports rising interest in CDs, drawing on figures from John Lewis and a music-and-film trends report. The fans it spoke to describe different reasons for returning to the format: some never left it, while others have turned to discs after finding vinyl bulky or streaming’s endless choices overwhelming.

segments.title: A more deliberate listen
segments.body: Several interviewees value owning music that might disappear from streaming services, and one buys directly from independent and folk musicians so they receive a larger share of the money. Others say a CD encourages attention to an album as a whole, without autoplay or algorithmic playlists. Not everyone rejects streaming: one collector uses it to discover music before buying discs.

content.headline: Satanic Planet’s Dead Deities makes provocation part of its noisy craft
content.shortHeadline: Satanic Planet make a noisy, provocative album
content.standfirst: The metal group led by Satanic Temple co-founder Lucien Greaves pairs political provocation with industrial noise, choral organs and precise, heavy arrangements. The review finds a compelling record, though not every lyric escapes its own edginess.

sources.originalTitle: Dead Deities

segments.body: Satanic Planet is a metal supergroup featuring producer Luke Henshaw, the Locust’s Justin Pearson and drummer Dave Lombardo. On Dead Deities, the band’s second album, Lucien Greaves brings the project’s political intent to music that moves between experimental metal, industrial textures and processed vocals.

segments.title: More than a provocation
segments.body: The review singles out the heavy organ and noisy textures of “Church Burning” and the tension-building arrangement of “Ouroboros”. It praises the group’s attention to sound as a reason the album avoids slipping into parody, while also calling the lyrics of “Sam Alito’s Mom” arguably misogynistic and questioning how fresh some of the record’s anti-authoritarian slogans feel.

content.headline: Olivia Tremor Control’s final album turns mortality into psychedelic pop
content.shortHeadline: Olivia Tremor Control’s final album faces mortality
content.standfirst: The Elephant 6 band’s first album in 27 years arrives after the deaths of founding members Bill Doss and Will Cullen Hart. Its familiar pop and sound collages now carry an unsettling weight, the review argues.

sources.originalTitle: The Same Place

segments.body: The Same Place, the Olivia Tremor Control’s third and final album, has been in progress since 2010. Most of it was recorded between 2010 and 2012; other members and collaborators added finishing touches after co-frontmen Bill Doss and Will Cullen Hart died.

segments.title: A familiar sound, newly shadowed
segments.body: The review hears the band’s characteristic pop instincts and sound-collage experiments, but with a persistent darkness around them. Songs that circle time and mortality—including the winding “The Spinning Continuous”—make the album feel newly poignant, without resolving the questions it raises. The result is both a return to a beloved band and a postscript to the Elephant 6 scene.

content.headline: Mackeeper turn aughts pop nostalgia into sly, finely made songs
content.shortHeadline: Mackeeper’s debut makes a game of pop nostalgia
content.standfirst: The New York duo’s first full-length reaches back to the pop-rock swagger of the 2000s, from guitar solos to boy-band melodies. The review finds that their teasing, self-aware approach is matched by serious craft.

sources.originalTitle: Believe You Me

segments.body: Mackeeper’s debut album, Believe You Me, draws on the duo’s upbringing with Top 40 music and music-production software. The review hears echoes of early-2000s pop, rap-rock and grunge, assembled into songs that are carefully arranged even when Cohen and Harwood play at being scraggly anti-heroes.

segments.title: The joke and the song
segments.body: Miles Cohen’s vocal shifts from boyish earnestness to a more forceful snarl, while “Men in Black” combines crunchy guitars, half-time drums and playful ad-libs. The critic’s central pleasure is the tension between the duo’s wink at pop conventions and their obvious skill at making hooks that work on their own terms.

content.headline: Kentridge’s Shostakovich animation finds black comedy in Soviet history
content.shortHeadline: Kentridge turns Shostakovich into a comic, dark ballet
content.standfirst: Oh to Believe in Another World pairs a collage animation and live choreography with Shostakovich’s 10th Symphony. The review sees the work’s humour as part of its response to Stalinist tyranny and the loss of revolutionary idealism.

image.caption: An image from William Kentridge’s Oh to Believe in Another World.

sources.originalTitle: Oh to Believe in Another World review – William Kentridge’s amazing animated ballet of black comic pain

segments.body: William Kentridge’s hour-long cine-musical uses masks, models, dancers and live-action choreography to accompany Shostakovich’s 10th Symphony. Its Soviet figures—including Stalin, Lenin, Trotsky and poet Vladimir Mayakovsky—move through meticulously built miniature settings that become, through the film’s effects, almost lifesize.

segments.title: A laugh with a shadow
segments.body: The review is struck by the work’s black comedy: Stalin’s monumental face remains fixed while the dancer beneath it capers. That humour sits alongside photographs of people targeted by the state and the symphony’s ambiguous mix of fear, revulsion and grief. For the critic, the film is shaped for the music, and its longing for another world mourns both lost idealism and what replaced it.

content.headline: Ten films beyond horror that can still leave viewers frightened
content.shortHeadline: Ten terrifying films that aren’t horror
content.standfirst: Guardian writers pick films that unsettle through human cruelty, social dread and the unknown rather than relying on the conventions of horror. Their choices range from The Hunchback of Notre Dame to 2001: A Space Odyssey.

image.caption: Mia McKenna-Bruce in How to Have Sex, one of the films in the selection.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I left shellshocked’: writers on their scariest non-horror movies

segments.body: The selection looks beyond the horror genre for films that frighten by other means. Its choices include the creeping menace of Lee Chang-dong’s Burning, the cruelty and bigotry in Disney’s The Hunchback of Notre Dame, and the dread of a young girl’s holiday in How to Have Sex.

segments.title: Dread in different forms
segments.body: Other writers point to 2001: A Space Odyssey’s fear of human technology, the grim investigation in The Sniper and the oppressive atmosphere of Dark Waters. The recommendations also include the anxiety of The Hunt, Zodiac and Requiem for a Dream, showing how suspense, injustice and human behaviour can unsettle as powerfully as monsters or jump scares.

content.headline: Wicker makes a strange romantic fantasy from a woman’s wish for kindness
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s odd romance has a serious argument beneath it
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who commissions a husband made of wicker, played by Alexander Skarsgård. An interview and a sharply dissenting review see the comic fantasy as both a challenge to convention and an uneasy story about his lack of agency.

image.caption: Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I saw the script and went: oooh!’ Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard on their steamy folk-horror movie Wicker
Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, a fisherwoman mocked by her village asks a basketmaker to make her a husband. The result is Skarsgård’s Wicker Husband, a creature devoted to her happiness. Colman and the film-makers describe the story as an earthy, bawdy fairy tale in which a woman who has little place in the village’s conventions gets to choose the shape of her own life.

segments.title: Fantasy and its limits
segments.body: The i Paper’s review enjoys the film’s comic, horny absurdity but argues that the Wicker Husband’s own wishes receive too little attention: his devotion is not the same as free choice. The Guardian interview emphasises the Fisherwoman’s agency and the film’s satire of patriarchal marriage. Together, the accounts capture the tension between the film’s playful wish-fulfilment and its questions about equality.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s critic argues that the film’s central joke has a troubling edge: the Wicker Husband is expected to serve his wife and accept danger, with little attention paid to his own desires.

content.headline: The Mosquito Bowl mixes football and war but leans on familiar heroics
content.shortHeadline: The Mosquito Bowl pairs war action with stale heroics
content.standfirst: Peter Berg’s Second World War drama links a football game among US marines with the battle of Okinawa. The review praises its absorbing action while questioning its clichés and the way Japanese suffering sits at the edge of the story.

image.caption: Nicholas Galitzine and Ray Nicholson in The Mosquito Bowl.

sources.originalTitle: The Mosquito Bowl review – Netflix mixes football, war and cliches in slick by-the-numbers saga

segments.body: The Mosquito Bowl follows college football players who joined the US marines after Pearl Harbor and a 1944 game on Guadalcanal. The review finds the action sequences effective, with the movement and camaraderie of sport giving the film a visual way to connect the football field with the battlefield.

segments.title: Whose war is shown?
segments.body: The critic finds the dialogue heavy with familiar speeches about honour and duty, and questions how the film balances period-accurate racism among US soldiers with its own point of view. Its emphasis on American suffering, the review argues, sits uneasily beside the largely unnamed anguish of Japanese soldiers and civilians at Okinawa.

content.headline: Elke Sommer, star of A Shot in the Dark, dies aged 85
content.shortHeadline: Elke Sommer, star of A Shot in the Dark, dies aged 85
content.standfirst: The German-born actor appeared in Hollywood films with Peter Sellers, Paul Newman and Dick Van Dyke, as well as British comedies and horror films. Bild magazine reported that she died in Los Angeles of heart failure.

image.caption: Elke Sommer, the German-born actor whose career spanned European and Hollywood films.

sources.originalTitle: Elke Sommer, prolific German star of A Shot in the Dark and And Then There Were None, dies aged 85

segments.body: Elke Sommer, whose roles included the maid suspected of murder in the Pink Panther sequel A Shot in the Dark, has died aged 85. Bild magazine reported that she died in Los Angeles of heart failure. Born Elke Schletz in Berlin, she was evacuated to Bavaria during the war and was spotted by Vittorio De Sica after winning a beauty contest in Italy.

segments.title: A career across languages
segments.body: Sommer’s gift for languages helped her move between Italian, German, British and Hollywood films. Her credits included The Prize with Paul Newman, And Then There Were None and Carry on Behind. In the 1970s she also appeared in two horror films by Mario Bava, before later concentrating on painting.

content.headline: Gentle Monster examines the loyalty that keeps women close to troubled men
content.shortHeadline: Gentle Monster asks what loyalty costs two women
content.standfirst: Marie Kreutzer’s drama follows a musician whose husband is under police investigation and a detective who makes excuses for her father. Its central tension lies in what remains unknown about the men they love.

image.caption: Léa Seydoux in Gentle Monster.

sources.originalTitle: Gentle Monster review – disquieting drama about two women facing the truth about the men they love

segments.body: Lucy Weiss, a French musician played by Léa Seydoux, has moved to the countryside to support her husband after his breakdown. Then detective Elsa arrives with a search warrant and removes his devices. The film follows Lucy’s struggle to understand what he has done, while Elsa pursues a case and avoids confronting her own father’s behaviour.

segments.title: The pain of not knowing
segments.body: The police find no evidence that Lucy’s son has been abused, but Elsa warns that certainty is impossible. Lucy, meanwhile, hears shifting explanations from her husband and tries to make them fit what she sees. The review calls this a bleak drama about loyalty and denial, anchored by Seydoux and Jella Haase’s contrasting performances.

content.headline: Twelve family-friendly films for a Halloween night with scares
content.shortHeadline: Twelve spooky films to watch with the family
content.standfirst: This Halloween guide offers a dozen films that aim to frighten without resorting to the most extreme horror. It ranges from Coraline and Goosebumps to The Others and Poltergeist, with a reminder to check the age ratings.

image.caption: A Halloween guide to scary films for family viewing.

sources.originalTitle: 12 scary films you can actually watch with your kids this Halloween

segments.body: The guide suggests films for families seeking a Halloween scare, while noting that parental discretion matters. Its choices include Coraline’s unsettling stop-motion fantasy, the comic creature chaos of Gremlins and the ghost story The Others, which finds its unease in atmosphere rather than explicit violence.

segments.title: For older viewers
segments.body: Other picks include The Woman in Black, The Sixth Sense and Poltergeist. The guide flags Crimson Peak as more suitable for older teens because of its bloody imagery and adult themes, and provides age-rating context to help families choose what fits their children.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning draws sharply different verdicts on Facebook’s harms
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning: chilling exposé or toothless drama?
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s film dramatises the Facebook Files, journalist Jeff Horwitz’s reporting on the company’s platform. One review finds an unsettling warning about social media’s hold on daily life; another says the drama lacks urgency and is unlikely to change minds.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆

segments.body: The Social Reckoning follows journalist Jeff Horwitz and whistleblower Frances Haugen as they uncover Facebook research and decisions tied to users’ wellbeing and political misinformation. Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg. The i Paper review says the film’s dark tone turns the investigation into a story about a system viewers are already part of.

segments.title: Two readings of its impact
segments.body: The i Paper writer finds the film frightening partly because the real-life revelations have become so familiar that people can grow numb to them. The BBC’s review reaches a less favourable verdict: it praises the opening and some of the reporting, but finds little tension, a limited Zuckerberg character and no real reckoning. The disagreement is over whether the film makes a compelling warning or an ineffective drama.

perspectives.body: The BBC critic argues that the film’s investigative premise never becomes a tense drama: Horwitz and Haugen are not threatened, and the story’s strands do not meaningfully converge.

content.headline: SCTV’s oddball sketch comedy gave a generation of stars its start
content.shortHeadline: How SCTV made room for comedy that refused to dumb down
content.standfirst: Dave Thomas recalls the Canadian sketch show that launched John Candy, Eugene Levy and Catherine O’Hara, and influenced The Simpsons. A new documentary and the release of 134 episodes bring its layered, low-budget comedy back into view.

image.caption: Members of SCTV’s cast, including Catherine O’Hara, John Candy and Eugene Levy.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It really was the idiots in charge’: inside the TV sketch show that launched a generation of stars

segments.body: Second City Television followed a run-down station in the fictional Canadian town of Melonville, making its limited budget part of the joke. Dave Thomas, an original cast member and head writer, says the show aimed high with its references and trusted viewers to keep up. Its cast also included John Candy, Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, Rick Moranis and Andrea Martin.

segments.title: Making the constraints work
segments.body: Thomas says the early show was a failure, but its makeshift look gave the writers room to build distinctive characters and interlocking parodies. The approach later influenced The Simpsons, whose writers admired SCTV’s layered comedy. Thomas is less impressed by the new documentary’s omissions, including its limited attention to the show’s writers and musical guests.

content.headline: Awkwafina returns to her family’s restaurant story in a personal cooking series
content.shortHeadline: Awkwafina explores family history through food
content.standfirst: In Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook, Nora Lum travels across the US to learn from Asian American chefs and consider whether her family restaurant can return. She talks about the show’s connection to her late grandmother and the restaurant’s place in her family history.

image.caption: Awkwafina, also known as Nora Lum, whose series follows her family’s restaurant history.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I felt bad for my exes’: Awkwafina on making deeply personal TV – with her grandma

segments.body: Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook follows Nora Lum as she learns from a new generation of Asian American chefs, with the hope of reviving her family’s long-closed Cantonese restaurant. Lum says the restaurant, opened by her great-grandfather in Flushing, Queens, helped bring the family to the US and remained a presence in family life after it closed in 1982.

segments.title: A family story on screen
segments.body: Lum describes the series as a love letter to her grandmother, who helped raise her after her mother died. She also reflects on the work and sacrifices behind restaurant life, including the family’s losses when her grandmother’s business failed. The show’s warm approach, she says, does not set out to make a political point, but immigrant experience is inseparable from the story of Chinese-American food.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors’ biggest turns—and the debate over James Acaster
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors: its best moments and Acaster’s exit
content.standfirst: A highlights roundup revisits the celebrity series’ mistakes, reversals and one-liners. A second account argues that James Acaster’s decision to confess as a Traitor drained the game of the tension viewers wanted.

image.caption: A moment from The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Game-breaking blunders, killer yawns … and a puddle of vomit: it’s the top 10 Celebrity Traitors moments
James Acaster has made a mockery of The Celebrity Traitors

segments.body: The Guardian’s countdown recalls the camp opening, Ross Kemp’s spiralling paranoia, Jerry Hall’s one-liners and the surprise of three Traitors receiving a special power. It also tracks the game’s volatile alliances and Acaster’s unusual decision to play against the role he had been given.

segments.title: A confession that split opinion
segments.body: The i Paper’s critic was frustrated when Acaster admitted he had been recruited as a Traitor and was “a Faithful at heart”. The piece argues that his confession cut short a tense confrontation and let the other players avoid fully testing their suspicions of Maya Jama. It reflects a different expectation of the format from the broader highlights roundup.

perspectives.body: The i Paper critic says Acaster’s early confession robbed the episode of a proper contest, arguing that players and viewers invest in seeing the Traitors pushed to defend themselves.

content.headline: Matthew Perry’s own memoir makes Netflix’s new documentary feel intrusive
content.shortHeadline: A Matthew Perry documentary revisits what he already told us
content.standfirst: The One About Matthew Perry draws on interviews with his family and archive footage, but the review argues that its retelling adds little to his own memoir. It finds the treatment of his death both cursory and painful for those close to him.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Matthew Perry documentary is undignified and intrusive

segments.body: The three-part documentary follows Perry from aspiring actor to Friends star and addiction campaigner, using archive footage and accounts from people close to him. The review finds parts of it moving, but notes that Perry had already described his addiction in detail in his 2022 memoir, Friends, Lovers and the Big Terrible Thing.

segments.title: What the documentary leaves out
segments.body: The critic says the film moves quickly past unresolved questions about Perry’s death and the people who supplied him with ketamine, instead lingering on relatives’ recollections of learning that he had died. The review questions whether that access serves viewers or Perry’s memory, while acknowledging the emotion of seeing his Friends castmates attend his funeral together.

content.headline: Call the Midwife’s Laura Main reflects on the show’s break and caring for her 91
content.shortHeadline: Laura Main on Call the Midwife, caring and a new role
content.standfirst: After 15 years on Call the Midwife, Laura Main is spending the show’s hiatus on stage and helping care for her mother. She discusses playing the Queen’s dresser and why she wanted Shelagh to age naturally.

image.caption: Laura Main, who plays the Queen’s dresser in By Royal Appointment.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I wanted my Call the Midwife character to age normally – even if I didn’t want to’

segments.body: Laura Main has not filmed Call the Midwife this year, as the BBC drama takes a break and prepares a prequel, Sisters in Arms. Main says she will miss the programme, where she has played Shelagh since 2012, but the pause has also allowed her to help care for her 91-year-old mother in Aberdeen.

segments.title: A different part to play
segments.body: Main is touring in By Royal Appointment, a play about Elizabeth II in which she plays the Queen’s dresser and confidant. She says she felt strongly that Shelagh should age at the character’s natural rate, even if she might prefer otherwise. She also describes the practical support her family received from Aberdeen council and worries that many carers have to leave paid work.

content.headline: After decades playing games, GamesMaster’s Dominik Diamond becomes one
content.shortHeadline: GamesMaster’s Dominik Diamond steps inside a game
content.standfirst: The broadcaster voices the hero of the indie survival horror game Black Tides: Draga’s Wake. He describes the strangeness of hearing himself in the role—and the moment his children realised their father was on screen.

image.caption: Draga, the protagonist voiced by Dominik Diamond in Black Tides: Draga’s Wake.

sources.originalTitle: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one

segments.body: After 50 years of playing video games, Dominik Diamond has taken a voice role in Black Tides: Draga’s Wake. The game is a survival horror story set aboard a decaying steamship after a heist goes wrong; Diamond voices Draga, a sailor infected by an ancient god.

segments.title: A personal performance
segments.body: Diamond says he initially disliked hearing his voice against the game’s powerful-looking hero, but found a quieter delivery that suited the character. Recording improvised fight sounds felt especially strange. His favourite moment came when he played clips to his children without telling them he was involved, then watched them recognise their father.

content.headline: Lara Croft at 30: the missteps behind gaming’s enduring icon
content.shortHeadline: Lara Croft at 30: the failures that couldn’t undo her
content.standfirst: The Tomb Raider anniversary prompts a look at the character’s worst games, awkward advertising and recurring attempts to recast her as a damsel. The feature argues that Lara’s appeal survived repeated failures to understand what made her compelling.

image.caption: Lara Croft in Tomb Raider IV–VI Remastered.

sources.originalTitle: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders

segments.body: Thirty years after Lara Croft’s debut, the feature looks beyond the series’ successes to its less celebrated decisions. It revisits the annual release schedule that wore down the original developers, the poorly received Tomb Raider: Chronicles and Angel of Darkness, and marketing that turned Lara into a product as much as a game character.

segments.title: The character beyond the image
segments.body: The article also criticises later games for giving Lara unnecessary sidekicks and for centring her vulnerability and sexualisation. It points to the 2013 reboot’s controversy over a trailer depicting an attempted assault, arguing that such choices missed the appeal of a capable, enigmatic solo adventurer. Despite them, Lara remains a major figure in games culture, with another adventure due next year.

content.headline: Pompeii wardrobe reveals jewellery, cosmetics and a child’s charm necklace
content.shortHeadline: Pompeii wardrobe yields a child’s necklace and daily treasures
content.standfirst: A cabinet sealed by the AD79 eruption held coins, cosmetics and a necklace traditionally worn by children. The finds offer a glimpse of household life in the ancient city—and suggest its occupants may have fled suddenly.

image.caption: Personal belongings uncovered in a Pompeii home on Via dell’Abbondanza.

sources.originalTitle: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe

segments.body: Archaeologists have found personal belongings—including tweezers, a perfume bottle, an incense burner and 38 bronze coins—in a wooden wardrobe in a Pompeii home. The cabinet was sealed when Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD79; the house stands on Via dell’Abbondanza, one of the city’s busiest streets.

segments.title: A child’s keepsake
segments.body: The most distinctive object is a necklace with more than 20 charms, including figures of the gods Bes and Mercury. Known as a crepundia, this kind of necklace was traditionally worn by children; its charms could rattle to help parents keep track of them and might also help identify a child.

Coins and personal objects left behind may mean the household had to escape at short notice, Gabriel Zuchtriegel, director of Pompeii archaeological park, said. Cooking pots and a box with lead weights also suggest someone in the home was a tradesperson; the discovery is part of a wider restoration project.

content.headline: Seabird ‘jet lag’ can send inexperienced shearwaters hundreds of miles off track
content.shortHeadline: Seabird jet lag may send young shearwaters far off course
content.standfirst: Twenty years of tracking data suggest Manx shearwaters can lose their bearings when rapid eastward flights put their body clocks out of sync with local time. Adults corrected small errors; first-time foragers may struggle more.

image.caption: A Manx shearwater, a seabird that navigates using the sun.

sources.originalTitle: Migrating seabirds face a surprising problem: jet lag

segments.body: Manx shearwaters returning to colonies off the west coast of the UK can be thrown off course after flying rapidly east across the Atlantic, a study of 20 years of GPS tracking data suggests. The change in local time can leave the birds’ internal clocks up to about an hour behind, disrupting their use of the sun to navigate.

segments.title: Experience matters
segments.body: Adult birds corrected their bearings in flight. Their errors added an estimated 5km to a 1,000km journey, according to the research. First-time foragers lack the same map sense to reorient themselves and could deviate by hundreds of kilometres, the researchers said.

The findings, published in Science, support the idea that the birds rely heavily on the sun as a compass: errors remained even when they followed coastlines, where landmarks might have helped. Richard Holland of Bangor University, who was not involved, called the finding significant, while noting that the consequences for birds that return to their colonies remain unclear.

content.headline: Venice lagoon was once dry land as sea levels reshaped the Adriatic
content.shortHeadline: Rising seas turned land around Venice into a lagoon
content.standfirst: Seismic data and sediment cores show that the present-day lagoon once extended more than 30 miles inland. Researchers say rising seas also transformed hills and wetlands across the northern Adriatic over thousands of years.

sources.originalTitle: How rising seas transformed dry land into Venice lagoon

segments.body: The land where Venice now stands was once dry ground many miles from the coast, according to a reconstruction of the northern Adriatic landscape over the past 10,000 years. Researchers combined seismic data with sediment cores from coastal basins in northern Italy, Slovenia and northern Croatia.

The study, published in Quaternary Science Reviews, indicates the present-day Venice lagoon once stretched more than 30 miles inland. Trieste, now a coastal city, was previously an area of hills overlooking swamps and lagoons.

Sea levels rose in fits and starts, at times by as much as 25mm a year. The changing coastline would have forced Mesolithic hunter-gatherers to adapt their hunting and fishing; a more stable period over the past 6,000 years helped settlements and farming take root.

content.headline: ‘Ferritin face’ symptoms may suggest low iron—but cannot diagnose it
content.shortHeadline: Can your face reveal low iron? Experts say a blood test is needed
content.standfirst: Pallor, dark circles and hair loss can have many causes, although low iron stores may contribute. Experts caution against treating social-media symptom lists as a diagnosis and advise checking levels with a blood test.

image.caption: A blood test can measure ferritin, a protein that stores iron.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction?

segments.body: Social media posts use “ferritin face” to describe pallor, dark circles, dry skin and hair loss as signs of low iron. Experts say iron deficiency can affect appearance, but these symptoms also have other possible causes, including genetics, stress and dehydration; a face alone cannot establish a diagnosis.

segments.title: Testing and causes
segments.body: Ferritin is a protein that stores iron, and its level can be measured with a blood test. NICE guidance cited in the reporting treats ferritin below 30 micrograms per litre as indicating iron deficiency; Oxford University Hospitals haematology professor Sue Pavord said a level below 50 might also be a pointer. Levels are not always a reliable guide on their own.

Heavy periods and pregnancy are common causes, while diet, poor absorption and blood loss can also contribute. Experts advise people at higher risk or concerned about symptoms to seek testing and assessment to establish the cause; self-diagnosis or supplements are not a substitute for that advice.

content.headline: Vascular dementia may be more common than assumed, experts say
content.shortHeadline: Vascular dementia may be under-recognised, experts say
content.standfirst: Blood-vessel damage may overlap with Alzheimer’s disease, complicating diagnosis and research. Specialists say controlling blood pressure and other vascular risks could help prevent some people with early memory problems from progressing to dementia.

image.caption: Researchers say damage to blood vessels may play a larger role in dementia than commonly recognised.

sources.originalTitle: The little-known blood pressure pill benefits that could be dementia game-changer

segments.body: Vascular dementia, usually estimated to account for 20–30% of dementia cases, may be under-recognised, including in people diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, according to experts interviewed by The i Paper. It results from damage to the brain’s blood vessels, which can follow a stroke or build gradually over time.

segments.title: An overlap in the brain
segments.body: Research suggests impaired blood vessels can hinder the clearance of waste from nerve cells and worsen the build-up of proteins such as amyloid. In turn, amyloid can accumulate in blood-vessel walls and restrict blood flow. University of Manchester clinician scientist Adam Greenstein said this means Alzheimer’s may also involve blood-vessel disease.

There is no guarantee that prevention measures will stop dementia, but experts say managing blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking and other vascular risks can reduce the chance of progression, particularly when memory problems are identified early. Two drugs already used to open blood vessels are also being tested in UK trials for vascular dementia; their effectiveness is not yet known.

content.headline: Longevity research claims face scrutiny over age records and ‘Blue Zones’
content.shortHeadline: Oxford demographer challenges popular longevity claims
content.standfirst: Demographer Saul Newman argues that shaky records undermine claims about extreme old age and so-called Blue Zones, while telomere research has not delivered the anti-ageing breakthrough once hoped for. The company behind Blue Zones disputes his assessment.

image.caption: Oxford demographer Saul Newman, who critiques claims about longevity research.

sources.originalTitle: I’m a longevity expert. These four anti-ageing myths are junk science

segments.body: Oxford demographer Saul Newman argues that some popular longevity claims rest on unreliable evidence. He says age records for people said to have reached 105 or more can lack reliable documentation, and that suspicious patterns in dates of birth raise doubts about some databases of the oldest people.

segments.title: Claims and evidence
segments.body: Newman also challenges the evidence behind “Blue Zones”—places promoted for unusually long lives—and says commercial promotion has run ahead of reliable data. A spokesperson for the company that licenses Blue Zones programmes said its content is scientifically validated and regularly reviewed; a spokesperson for researcher Dan Buettner said Newman’s work had been disproven by peer-reviewed research.

Newman says telomere shortening is now understood as part of a more complex picture of ageing, not a simple route to extending life. He also points to the risks and lack of proven benefit in young-blood transfusions, which the US Food and Drug Administration has warned have no established clinical benefit for preventing ageing or memory loss.

content.headline: Binance says $6.3bn in crypto was affected by record breach; probe continues
content.shortHeadline: Binance breach affects $6.3bn in crypto; investigation continues
content.standfirst: Binance says the incident affected $6.3bn in digital assets and that industry partners have frozen about $3bn. The exchange has pledged to cover losses, but the attack’s route and the identity of those responsible remain under investigation.

image.caption: Binance is the cryptocurrency exchange at the centre of the breach investigation.

sources.originalTitle: Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
North Korean group blamed for $6.3bn Binance hack in biggest ever crypto heist
Binance hackers stole $6.3 billion in record-breaking crypto heist
‘Largest Crypto Hack in History’: Binance Loses More Than $6B
North Korean hackers blamed for stealing record $6.3B in Binance breach

segments.body: Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, says $6.3bn in digital assets was affected in what researchers describe as the largest known crypto theft. The company says about $3bn has been frozen and it will cover customer losses. Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while it secured its systems and traced the funds.

segments.title: How the breach may have happened
segments.body: Binance’s initial investigation pointed to a compromised employee laptop, but the company later reported additional breach points. It says it has found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked and has not attributed responsibility to an individual. How the laptop was compromised and how the wider attack unfolded remain unclear.

segments.title: Attribution remains unconfirmed
segments.body: Blockchain analysis firms including TRM Labs, Chainalysis and Elliptic have linked the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group, but Binance has not confirmed that attribution. The exchange says it is working with law enforcement and industry partners to identify those responsible and recover additional assets.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that the Bank of England and UK Financial Conduct Authority are monitoring possible effects on firms exposed to Binance, though the Bank is understood to have no active concerns.

content.headline: Migrant workers report dangerous conditions on Europe’s data-centre sites
content.shortHeadline: Investigation finds migrant workers at risk on data-centre builds
content.standfirst: A Guardian and Investigate Europe investigation documents alleged unsafe work, overcrowded housing, unpaid wages and a tuberculosis case at sites in four countries. Contractors and technology companies say they have safety and labour standards in place.

image.caption: Illustration accompanying an investigation into conditions for workers building data centres in Europe.

sources.originalTitle: Electrocutions, disease and no pay: how workers risk exploitation in Europe’s datacentres

segments.body: A five-month investigation by The Guardian and Investigate Europe found accounts of serious injuries, unsafe work, poor accommodation and pay disputes involving migrant workers building data centres in Sweden, Norway, Belgium and the Netherlands. One electrical tester, identified as Sandu, says he was badly burned in an accident at a Google site in Belgium.

segments.title: Living and pay conditions
segments.body: Workers at a Microsoft project in Gävle showed reporters evidence of crowded housing and said they had encountered vermin, broken ventilation and inadequate heating. Medical records documented a worker with active tuberculosis, though public authorities said no outbreak had been reported. More than 30 workers also presented payslips that appeared to show unpaid overtime and missed holiday pay.

The investigation says a union settlement with subcontractor BenBau provided for back pay and union access to sites. BenBau, Collen, Dornan Engineering, Google and Microsoft described commitments or procedures for worker safety, labour-law compliance and welfare. No company or contractor appears to have been found liable for Sandu’s accident; the local labour inspectorate closed its investigation without finding wrongdoing.

content.headline: Court filing says Meta staff discussed a ‘whisper strategy’ against Jonathan Ha\
content.shortHeadline: Meta staff discussed undermining critic Jonathan Haidt, records show
content.standfirst: Meeting notes in a US legal filing record staff discussing how to turn academics against the author of The Anxious Generation. The documents do not show whether Meta acted on the ideas, and the company has not commented.

image.caption: Jonathan Haidt, whose work on social media and young people is discussed in the court filing.

sources.originalTitle: Meta discussed ‘whisper strategy’ against social media critic Jonathan Haidt, files show

segments.body: Internal meeting notes included in a US court filing show Meta employees discussing a “whisper strategy” to undermine Jonathan Haidt, the social psychologist whose book The Anxious Generation argues that smartphones have contributed to a youth mental-health crisis. The notes refer to getting academics to disavow him and to a “below-the-line” campaign.

segments.title: What the documents establish
segments.body: The notes date from March 2023, before Haidt published the book, and relate to responding to a Substack post reviewing research. They suggest staff discussed seeking a critical article, but it is not clear whether Meta acted on the ideas. A person referred to as “Gellman” is not identified in the document; statistician Andrew Gelman said he was never hired to write a hit piece.

Haidt said he was not surprised by the discussions, adding that companies may go after a messenger when they cannot dispute the evidence. Meta had been approached for comment, according to the report.

content.headline: Waymo and Toyota plan to test robotaxis in Japan before wider rollout
content.shortHeadline: Waymo and Toyota plan Japan robotaxi tests next year
content.standfirst: Toyota will build electric bZ4X vehicles fitted with Waymo’s self-driving system for tests in Japan, with the companies also eyeing other right-hand-drive markets. A commercial service and any use in personally owned cars remain future possibilities.

sources.originalTitle: Waymo taps Toyota to supply robotaxis for Japan and the UK

segments.body: Waymo and Toyota plan to begin testing autonomous versions of Toyota’s electric bZ4X in Japan next year. Toyota is to build the 2027 vehicles and integrate Waymo’s self-driving system at its Takaoka factory, as the companies pursue robotaxi operations in international markets.
